Introducing 100 Things to know about Resilience Engineering

The Resilience in Software Foundation is launching a series on key concepts to understand in resilience engineering. There’s so much to understand in the field that it can feel overwhelming. Each short article explains a concept with links on where to read more.

The first article gives four different ways to think about resilience.

I won’t automatically include every article in the series here in the newsletter, but I’ll showcase the ones I find especially interesting to help keep the series at top of mind.

  Resilience in Software Foundation



Constraints and production pressure at eMudhra

The eMudhra CA key incident report is out, and it’s full of systemic issues and non-technical motivators. Here’s Lorin’s take on it.

  Lorin Hochstein



Key Autoscaling Metric #5: Two and a Half Replicas

A well-functioning autoscaler will minimize application churn without preventing the necessary scaling behavior your platform needs to serve your customers.

  Ian O’Gorman — Applied Computing Research Labs



Don’t restrict your incident commander pool to engineering managers

Some of the best ICs I’ve worked with were project managers, customer support representatives, and salespeople. Their perspective can be incredibly valuable and make them more effective at Incident Command than engineers.

  Brent Chapman



How we continuously validate formal specifications in production

Not only do they use verified formal specifications for a production service, they have monitoring and alerting for deviations from the model. Cool!

  Nicolas Couvrat — Datadog



Designing a reliable unplanned failover

Neki’s Admin system does not know whether the primary has failed or is merely unreachable from where Admin happens to run.

  Shlomi Noach — Planetscale



Why Your RCAs Aren’t Working

Four common areas that incident analysis can fall short, how to identify them, and what you can do. Tag yourself, I’m #4, or at least some organizations I’ve been in are.

  Oakley Hall



Phantasialand chlorine incident at Ling Bao hotel pool

A chlorine dosing system failed, 15 guests were injured, and this week’s Outlook outage was a contributing factor. This is our regular reminder that the systems we operate can be safety-critical even if we don’t realize it.

  KarloBag.eu

What does it cost to declare an incident?

I’ve seen this so many times. If declaring an incident gets in the way of responding to it, something’s wrong.

  Hugo van der Horst



300 Requests in 5 Minutes: How We Chose the Web Application Firewall (WAF) Limit for the Token Route

They have a maximum concurrency in Lambda, and they want to ensure that no one misbehaving client can exhaust it on its own.

  Daniil Romashov



GCP Incident details: europe-west2, 2026-10-19

This one’s really interesting. The PLC refused to enable generators because the standby utility power was live. However, that standby utility power couldn’t be used because the breaker was purposefully opened during maintenance. I’m sure thorough failure testing was completed, it’s just that this kind of scenario hadn’t occurred to them.

  Google



Why incident resolution time isn’t something you should target

The fire service doesn’t track mean time to put out a fire.  Why should we measure our MTTR?

  Brent Chapman



The Ubuntu 26.04 Rust sudo is not compatible with standard sudo

Wow. Between this, the difficulty in reverting back to standard coreutils, and ubuntu’s schedule in publishing a fix for CVE-2026-98432, I’m having some second thoughts on Ubuntu. And no, Chris, I don’t think you should be expected to file a bug report the sudo-rs stuff.

  Chris Siebenmann



Quick thoughts about the eMudhra incident

It’s like the security equivalent of Lorin’s law: a new process put in place with the goal of improving security (for a subset of users) itself was a the core of a security incident.

I’m really looking forward to uMudhra’s incident report, due tomorrow.

  Lorin Hochstein



Message Queues

An overview of queues and what they’re good for with a reliability engineering lens.

  Alex Ewerlöf



If The Above Does Not Work

Runbook as hand-off mechanism. Runbook as a pointer to who knows more. Runbook as an embodiment of hard-earned lessons from the past. This one has me thinking about runbooks in new ways.

  Tim Irving

Post-incident action items don’t deserve special treatment

Archaeological layers of P0 incident action items? There’s a better way.

  Brent Chapman



A Decade of Blame Awareness

Wow, the original for this article was one I included all the way back in issue #16. I think I’ve quoted the concepts from that one a million times.

  J. Paul Reed



We gave cloud agents a phone to QA

At incident.io, agents now go beyond coding their mobile app changes, they actually run the app in a simulator and provide visual evidence of the change for a human to review.

  Grayson Ho — incident.io



How to Survive Database Failover – Debezium and PostgreSQL in Production

Getting Debezium to stream the first PostgreSQL change into Kafka is straightforward; keeping it correct through failover is the interesting part.

  Frane Jelavic — ShiftMag



The Titanic didn’t sink for just one reason

This one shows the drawbacks of focusing on a root cause through a really cool lens: a Five Whys analysis of the sinking of the Titanic.

  Steve Mynett — Rootly



The Thin Orchestrator: How We Made Our AI Agents More Reliable by Giving the Router Less to Do

Giving an agent more context can make it less effective. Here’s Meta’s technique to mitigate that.

  Plawan Rath, Akhil Jindal and Ashwini Verma — Meta



The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructure

Migrating the busiest 0.00001% of repositories to Azure took some careful work and consideration of bottlenecks.

  Eleanor White and Victoria Dye — GitHub



What a room of engineers asked me about realtime resilience

My favorite section is the one about achieving higher reliability by coordinating between their client library and the server side.

  Matt Hammond — Ably
